FET DC Bias: JFET, D-MOSFET and E-MOSFET Q-points

Why this matters in the exam: FET DC bias is the whole of Week 7 (Module 3). It is also the first step of every FET amplifier question in Weeks 8–9, because you need before you can find . Ten of the questions in WS8 and WS9 (WS8 Q1–6, WS9 Q1–4) are pure bias questions. The practice test only covers Weeks 1–5, so there is no past paper evidence for marks. Expect the final to weight FETs heavily. Expect a bias question worth roughly 6–10 marks, either on its own or as part (a) of an amplifier question.

1. The core ideas

Three facts hold for every FET bias circuit:

E-MOSFET (n-channel) , with () Using , which an E-MOSFET does not have. Find first.

Saturation (pinch-off) check. Shockley’s equation and the square law only hold in the saturation region:

If this check fails, the device is in the ohmic region and your Q-point is wrong. An E-MOSFET with drain feedback always passes, because .

Graphical vs mathematical. The two methods give the same answer. The graph reads to about V and mA. The slides use the graph, for example mA in the common-gate example. The quadratic gives exact values, for example mA. Use the quadratic unless the question says “graphically” or “sketch”.

2. The method

Recognise the question type

  1. Look at the gate. Is it tied to a battery through ? That is fixed bias. Is it tied to ground through , with a resistor in the source? That is self-bias, or common gate if the signal enters at the source. Is it fed by /? That is voltage divider. Is connected from drain to gate? That is drain feedback (E-MOSFET).
  2. Look at the symbol and the data. If you are given and , it is a JFET or D-MOSFET. If you are given , and , it is an E-MOSFET.
  3. Read what is asked. “Find ” is analysis (Playbook A). “Find (or ) to give…” is design (Playbook B). “Given a measured voltage…” is reverse analysis (Playbook C).

Playbook A: find the Q-point

  1. Find . It is for fixed bias, for self-bias and common gate, and the divider value for voltage divider. Ignore , because no current flows in it.
  2. Write the bias line, (or the version from the table).
  3. Mathematical: substitute the bias line into the device equation. Expand into . Solve, or use the calculator equation solver. You get two roots.
  4. Choose the valid root. Work out for each root. For a JFET keep the root with . For a D-MOSFET keep the root with . For an E-MOSFET keep the root with . The other root always lies on the “mirror” half of the parabola and is not physical.
  5. Graphical: plot about 4 points of the transfer curve. Plot the bias line from its two intercepts. Read off the crossing.
  6. Output side: find , and .
  7. Do the saturation check (or ). State the result in one line.

Set V_G to 1.82 V to reproduce Example 1 (I_DQ ≈ 2.4 mA), then raise V_G and watch the Q-point climb the curve.

Playbook B: design for a target

  1. A target gives . A target is given directly.
  2. Invert the device equation to get . For a JFET, . For an E-MOSFET, .
  3. From the bias line, . Then (or with a negative supply).
  4. For a target , use .
  5. Check saturation with the designed values. A design that leaves the FET in the ohmic region does not work.

Playbook C: measured voltage given

A measured gives at once. A measured gives from the output KVL. Then . If is unknown, rearrange Shockley: .

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Keeping both roots, or the wrong one. Always compute for each root and reject the one outside (JFET), (D-MOSFET) or (E-MOSFET). Write one line saying why you rejected it.
  • Sign of . In WS8 Fig. 1 and Fig. 2, the battery’s + terminal is at ground, so is negative. Read the battery polarity, do not assume it.
  • Dropping a voltage across . , so (even 10 MΩ) has zero volts across it.
  • Forgetting the negative supply. With returned to , and when the gate is grounded. Do not use .
  • Units in the quadratic. Work in mA and kΩ, which gives volts directly. Mixing Ω with mA puts a factor of 1000 into and .
  • Stopping the D-MOSFET curve at . The Q-point can be at positive with (Example 2).
  • Using for an E-MOSFET. Compute from and first.
  • Skipping the saturation check. Two WS questions (WS8 Q5 and WS9 Q4) give a “textbook” answer that fails it. A one-line check earns marks and catches impossible results such as a negative .

WS9 Q4 (course question). For the network of Fig. 4, determine: (a) and and (b) and .

Solution

Reading the figure: this is an n-channel D-MOSFET (continuous channel bar). The gate is grounded. kΩ goes to +18 V. kΩ goes to −4 V. mA, V.

Standard method:

, so .

Substitute: . The roots are:

  • mA, which gives V. Reject it.
  • mA, which gives V. This is allowed for a D-MOSFET.

  1. mA, V.

  2. V. V. So V.

This result is impossible. cannot be negative for an n-channel device biased this way. The largest current the resistors can pass is mA, which happens when . That is less than the 9.01 mA that Shockley’s equation predicts. So the saturation check fails, and the MOSFET is in the ohmic region.

An ohmic-region (triode) model, which is not part of this course, gives about mA, V, V and V. You cannot do this calculation with this course’s tools.

What to write in an exam: give the Shockley values for (a). For (b), state V, then add that this violates , so the device is not in saturation and the Shockley Q-point is not valid. I believe this is the textbook problem the question is taken from. Its answer is usually quoted without this check, so the intended answer is probably mA, V, V, V.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

FET DC BIAS  (I_G = 0, I_D = I_S, no drop across R_G; work in mA and kOhm)
JFET/D-MOS:  I_D = IDSS(1 - VGS/VP)^2      E-MOS: I_D = k(VGS - VT)^2,
             VGS = VP(1 - sqrt(ID/IDSS))          k = ID(on)/(VGS(on) - VT)^2
Sketch: VGS = 0, 0.3VP, 0.5VP, VP  ->  ID = IDSS, IDSS/2, IDSS/4, 0
Bias lines:  fixed   VGS = -VGG
             self    VGS = -ID*RS
             divider VGS = VG - ID*RS,  VG = R2*VDD/(R1+R2)
             CG/-VSS VGS = VSS - ID*RS   (VS = -VSS + ID*RS)
             E-MOS drain feedback  VGS = VDS = VDD - ID*RD
Output:  VD = VDD - ID*RD,  VDS = VD - VS
Method:  bias line -> sub into device eqn -> quadratic -> keep root with
         VP <= VGS <= 0 (JFET), VGS >= VP (D-MOS, can be +), VGS > VT (E-MOS)
Design:  target VD -> ID = (VDD-VD)/RD;  ID -> VGS (invert);
         VS = VG - VGS;  RS = VS/ID;  RD = (VDD - VD)/ID
ALWAYS CHECK SATURATION: VDS >= VGS - VP  (E-MOS: VDS >= VGS - VT)
  Fails (or VDS < 0) -> ohmic region, Shockley Q-point not valid; say so.
